extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and legal practitioners (and advanced law students) handling patent damages and equity actions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing damages and drafting/prosecuting bills in equity in patent litigation, including when increased damages or injunctions are appropriate and the pleading content required under equity practice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to award increased damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased damages may properly be awarded by a court, ... in order to prevent a defendant infringer from profiting from his own wrong, whether that wrong was intentional or was unwitting. The power conferred by the statute is general. It is not confined to awarding punitive damages, but is to be exercised 'according to the circumstances of the case.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased (exemplary) damages are discretionary and aim to prevent unjust enrichment of infringers; they are not forfeitures. The statute's grant is broad — the court should consider the specific circumstances of each case in deciding whether to award increased damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating circumstances justifying increased damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That power will be exercised where the defendant's infringement was deliberate and intentional, ... or where the defendant acted in bad faith, or has been stubbornly litigious, or has caused unnecessary trouble and expense to the plaintiff; but not merely because the defendant's defence was so extensive as to require great expenditure to overcome it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting an award of increased damages include deliberate/intentional infringement, bad faith, persistent litigiousness, and causing unnecessary trouble/expense. Excessive but legitimate defense effort alone is insufficient to justify exemplary damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unawareness of patent does not excuse liability for actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict for actual damages cannot be averted by evidence that the defendant was ignorant of the existence of the patent at the time he infringed. All infringers have constructive notice of all patents, because all letters patent are recorded in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule analogizes constructive notice of patents to notice of land records or laws; lack of subjective knowledge of a patent is not a defense to recovering actual damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate continued infringement after validity established
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the infringer has deliberately and persistently infringed the patent after its validity has been established is sufficient to cause all doubts on question of fact to be resolved against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-decisional or post-establishment continued infringement is heavily disfavored and will tip factual disputes against the infringer for purposes of damages and equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees and litigation expenses excluded from actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither counsel fees nor any other expenses incident to litigation, can be included in a verdict for actual damages in a patent case. Certain expended fees may be recovered as costs by either; but no expenditures or costs can be recovered as damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation costs might be recoverable as costs under appropriate rules but must not be claimed as part of actual damages for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on royalties when royalty is measure of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest should be allowed on royalties, from the time those royalties ought to have been paid, in all cases where a royalty is the measure of the plaintiff's damages. No interest is due on damages measured otherwise than by a royalty, because such damages are unliquidated until they are ascertained by an action, except where the method of measurement is as definite and conclusive as in the case of a royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where damages are liquidated by a royalty measure, interest runs from when royalties were due; for unliquidated damages (non-royalty measures), interest is not generally appropriate unless the measurement is comparably definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent statutory damages measure and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for infringement of a design patent are fixed by a special statute, at the minimum amount of two hundred and fifty dollars, and at a maximum amount enough larger than that, to equal the total profit made by the infringer upon the infringing article or articles made or sold by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute sets floor ($250) and ceiling (infringer's profits) for design-patent damages. Courts have interpreted whether the statutory minimum applies per-infringement, per-claim, or per-patent differently — practitioners should be aware of circuit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge requirement to recover under design-patent statute
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to recover under this statute, the plaintiff must show that the defendant knew of the plaintiff's design, and knew of the plaintiff's patent, or at least knew of facts which put him upon his inquiry for that patent; and that he knew that the design was applied to the infringing article, without the license of the owner of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of the defendant's knowledge (or facts prompting inquiry) and that the design was used on the infringing article is required; against manufacturers knowledge may be presumed, but against dealers proof is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction in patent cases — scope and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction of equity in patent litigation is conferred upon the same courts that are authorized to exercise jurisdiction at law ... The principal function of actions in equity in such cases is to restrain future infringements of patents by means of the writ of injunction. In every case where an injunction is proper, a court of equity, in order to avoid a multiplicity of actions, will take an account of the profits which the defendant derived from infringing the complainant's patent, and will compel the defendant to pay that amount to the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity primarily grants injunctive relief and ancillary accounting for profits; equity also provides relief where legal remedies are inadequate, difficult, or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity may assess damages and follows legal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever equity has jurisdiction to decree an account of the defendant's profits, it also has jurisdiction to assess the damages which the complainant sustained on account of the defendant's infringement. In assessing damages, equity follows the law, and is guided by the rules and principles which are set forth in Chapter XIX of this book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts in equity apply the same substantive rules for damages as at law; when both profits and damages are ascertained, equity will enter decrees according to which exceeds the other, with potential for decrees not exceeding three times damages where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only earned portion of royalties should be assessed in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: But where damages are measured by a royalty, only the earned portion of the royalty should be assessed; for if the royalty assessed is one which covers the future life of the patent, its recovery would authorize a continuance of the defendant's doings, and thus defeat an injunction, and perhaps oust the jurisdiction of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity must avoid awarding future royalties that would effectively permit continued infringement; assess only royalties covering the period earned to the time of recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to impound infringing articles on preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prima facie case of infringement has been made out on a motion for a preliminary injunction, the court has power to impound in the custody of the marshal or of a receiver such infringing articles as may be in the possession of the defendant, but the court cannot order them destroyed before interlocutory decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctive relief can include seizure/impoundment to preserve the status quo; destruction prior to interlocutory decree is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be complainant in equity for patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant ... may be the holder of the complete title to that patent in the territory where the infringement occurred. Where the legal title resides in one person and the equitable title in another, both should generally join in such an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally both legal and equitable title holders should join; exceptions permit omission of one party where circumstances show a decree against the other is pleadable against the omitted holder, or where the equitable owner has a limited share or power to sue alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant with unissued patent cannot obtain injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: No grounds for a suit in equity to enjoin the use by a defendant of complainant's invention lies in favor of an applicant whose patent has not issued, even though the defendant has fraudulently secured a patent to himself for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only issued patents (or holders of legal title) can typically obtain injunctions; mere applicants lack standing for equitable injunctive relief even in face of third-party fraudulently obtained patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be defendant in equity patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant in an action in equity for an infringement of a patent may generally be any person or private corporation connected with that infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party and joinder issues (public corporations, joint infringers, etc.) are governed by general principles treated in the chapter on courts, parties, and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content requirements for an original bill (Equity Rule 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hereafter it shall be sufficient that a bill in equity shall contain, in addition to the usual caption: First, the full name, when known, of each plaintiff and defendant, and the citizenship and residence of each party... Second, a short and plain statement of the grounds upon which the court's jurisdiction depends. Third, a short and simple statement of the ultimate facts upon which the plaintiff asks relief... Fourth, if there are persons other than those named as defendants, who appear to be proper parties, the bill should state why they are not made parties... Fifth, a statement of and prayer for any special relief pending the suit on final hearing... If special relief pending the suit be desired the bill should be verified by the oath of the plaintiff, or someone having knowledge of the facts upon which such relief is asked."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity Rule 25 replaced many ancient formal parts; a bill must provide party identification, jurisdictional grounds, concise ultimate facts (not mere evidence), explain omission of necessary parties, and state/petition for interim relief; verification required if seeking special interim relief (e.g., preliminary injunction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal title and introductory part of the bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the court, at the beginning of a bill, should be in the same form as at the beginning of a declaration. The introductory part contains a formal address to the judges of the court ... together with the names, residences, and the citizenship of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical formality is recommended though practical convenience (entitling bill in the name of the case) is acceptable; introductory part must identify parties and their domiciles/citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for the stating part of a bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The stating part ... must state that the complainant fears and has reason to fear, future infringement by the defendant. It need not state past infringement, where it states a specific reason for fearing future infringement. Where profits are sought to be recovered, it must plainly aver that profits were realized by the defendant on account of the stated infringement, and that the infringements complained of, or some of them took place within six years before the filing of the bill. Where either damages or profits or both are sought to be recovered the bill must show proper marking under Section 4900 of the Revised Statutes or proper notice to the defendant, otherwise no recovery can be had except for infringements after suit commenced. The filing of the bill is notice. The bill should also allege infringements in all places where they have taken place...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating part must allege fear of future infringement (for injunctions), specify profits realized when seeking an accounting, respect six-year limitation on recoverable acts, plead statutory marking/notice requirements to recover pre-suit damages, and allege geographic scope of infringements to preserve recovery in those locales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent formalities and specification of claims in the bill
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in equity ... must show compliance with Section 4886 ... that the invention had not been previously patented or described in a printed publication, that the patentee is the original inventor, and ... title in the complainant. Furthermore, it must allege that the patent was issued in the name of the United States and under the seal of the Patent Office and that it was signed by the Commissioner of Patents. ... The purport of the patent is properly embodied in a bill of complaint, by making profert therein, of the patent on which the bill is based. But the particular claims of the patent which the complainant intends to prosecute in the case, must be specified by their numbers in the stating part of the bill of complaint. If, however, the bill charges infringement of 'the claims' of the patent in suit, it will be construed to charge infringement of all the claims...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plead statutory prerequisites (e.g., prior use, novelty, inventorship, title) and patent issuance formalities unless profert is used; specify claim numbers you will press (or be prepared that alleging 'the claims' will be deemed to allege all claims). Modern Rule 25 practice may permit shorter allegations (issuance and chain of title).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special pleading points: licensees, joint defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bill is brought by an owner of a patent for the benefit of a licensee it should so state as, if the bill apparently proceeds for the interest of the owner alone, no damages can be recovered on behalf of the licensee. Where a plurality of defendants are sued for infringing a patent, the bill ought to state that the infringement was joint, though it has also been held that the point may properly be left to implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the interest of any licensee beneficiary when suing for their benefit; where multiple defendants exist, allege joint infringement (or be prepared to rely on implication in jurisdictions that permit it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer for relief must be both special and general
rubrics_metrics.description: The prayer for relief should be both special and general. The special part should ask for a preliminary injunction, and for a permanent injunction, and for an account of the defendant's profits, and for an assessment of the complainant's damages, and for an increase of those damages, and for costs. The prayer for general relief should be in the ordinary form of prayers of that kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific requests for interim and permanent injunctive relief, accounting, damages (and treble/increased damages if appropriate), costs; also include the usual general relief clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories and discovery practice (legacy principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the interrogating part of the bill has been abolished ... the general principles of interrogatories have not been affected ... The interrogating part was designed to secure ... admissions or statements ... The character, but not the extent, of those doings, could properly be the subject ... If infringement was denied the defendant could not be compelled to state in answer to interrogatories how many of the infringing articles he has made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary practice separates interrogatories from the bill, but classic principles remain: interrogatories must be specific, may be divided and numbered, and cannot force an admission of matters in genuine dispute (e.g., quantity made if infringement denied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process, signature, and verification requirements for bills
rubrics_metrics.description: The prayer for process formerly had to contain the names of all the defendants ... The bill must be signed by one or more solicitors of record. An oath of the truth of the bill must be appended to such a document, if it prays for a preliminary injunction. Such an oath is to be made by the complainant or someone having knowledge of the facts ... Where the complainant is a corporation, the bill may be verified by an officer of the corporation who knows it to be true; ... Where there is a plurality of complainants, the bill may be sufficiently verified by the oath of one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper statutory/process allegations (where required), sign bills through counsel, and verify when seeking interim relief — corporate verification by an informed officer or agent is acceptable; one complainant's oath can suffice for multiple complainants.
